analysis.title: U.S. Home Prices Rise Further in August Amid Tight Inventory (S&P Cotality Case-Shiller HPI)
key_insights: The seasonally adjusted S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index rose 0.28% m/m in August, its fourth consecutive monthly increase.
National prices were up 2.1% y/y in August, an acceleration from late 2025 and early 2026. Annual growth hit its slowest pace since mid-2012 in February 2026, at 0.84%.

Prices rose m/m in 13 of 19 metro areas after seasonal adjustment. The largest gains were San Diego (+0.73%), Portland (+0.51%) and New York (+0.48%). Six metros fell, led by Las Vegas (-0.33%), Seattle (-0.15%) and Dallas (-0.14%).

On a y/y basis prices were up in 14 metros, led by Chicago (+6.70%), New York City (+6.19%) and Cleveland (+4.29%). Five metros were down, led by Seattle (-1.96%), Las Vegas (-1.29%) and Dallas (-0.79%).
Detroit's August data was not released because of a county-level recording office delay. Detroit's index fell 0.23% in July.

NAR existing single-family inventory was 1.57 million units in August, up from the 2022 record low of 0.74 million but below the 2.2 million historical average. Months' supply was 4.8, above pre-pandemic peak levels. Inventory rose 4.6% y/y in September.
Inventory shortages are most pronounced in major Northeastern metros, including Greater New York, which supports m/m price gains there.

Affordability, measured by mortgage payments relative to incomes, is near its lowest level since the 1980s, below the level of the 2000s housing boom. Prices remain more than 50% above pre-pandemic levels.
PNC expects low affordability, rising inventories and weak job growth to weigh on annual price growth in the near term, with risks tilted to the downside given the ongoing Iran conflict.

The typical 30-year fixed mortgage rate has risen from slightly below 6% before U.S. military action against Iran to above 7.3%. PNC expects mortgage rates to stay above 6.5% partly because markets are pricing higher expected inflation into long-term rates.
